title.title: A power saving for square-difference-free sets
title.subtitle: Claim: a set in $\{1, \dots, N\}$ with no square difference has at most $C N^{1-c}$ elements

plain: Pick numbers up to N with no two differing by a perfect square: you must leave out almost all of them

panels.caption: $\{1, 3, 6, 8\}$: no two elements differ by a perfect square

beats.text: How large can a set in $\{1, \dots, N\}$ be if no two elements differ by a square?
At least $N^{0.75}$; upper bounds only saved $e^{-c\sqrt{\log N}}$ (Green–Sawhney)
The claim: a fixed power saving, $|A| \le C N^{1-c}$

steps: Keep only the set's simplest rhythms, its rational frequencies
Build a positive score that controls the density
Each pass to shorter square steps shrinks it by a power of $N$
